details.airportInfo: Charles de Gaulle is the main international gateway to Paris. RER line B runs from the airport into the city and stops at Luxembourg, a short walk from the Sorbonne.
details.funFact: The Sorbonne takes its name from the College of Sorbonne, founded around 1253 by Robert de Sorbon. Today's building is a late-19th-century reconstruction, but Cardinal Richelieu's domed chapel from the 1600s still stands in its courtyard.
details.languageInfo: French is the language of lectures and daily life. The Latin Quarter got its name from the Latin once spoken by the university's medieval scholars.
details.transportationFact: The Latin Quarter is compact and easy to walk. Cluny–La Sorbonne metro station and Luxembourg RER station are both a few minutes from the Sorbonne.

buildings.name: The Sorbonne
buildings.description: The building that gave the University of Paris its nickname has housed scholars since the College of Sorbonne opened here in 1253. Henri-Paul Nénot's grand reconstruction wraps a ceremonial courtyard, a peristyle and the Grand Amphitheatre, all still shared by the university's successor institutions.
buildings.oldUse: College of Sorbonne / University of Paris
buildings.newUse: Shared seat of the University of Paris's successor universities

buildings.name: Sorbonne Chapel
buildings.description: Jacques Lemercier designed this domed chapel for Cardinal Richelieu's rebuilding of the College of Sorbonne, and Richelieu's tomb lies beneath the dome. It is the only building left from that 17th-century campus; the rest was replaced in the 1800s.
buildings.newUse: Historic chapel (mostly closed since a 1999 storm)

buildings.name: Sainte-Geneviève Library
buildings.description: Henri Labrouste's reading room is a landmark of iron architecture: sixteen slender cast-iron Ionic columns carry openwork iron arches beneath twin barrel vaults. Facing the Panthéon, it is the main inter-university library of the universities of Paris.
buildings.oldUse: Library of the Abbey of Saint Genevieve's collection

buildings.name: École de Médecine
buildings.description: Built as the Academy of Surgery, Jacques Gondouin's building was the home of the Faculty of Medicine of Paris from 1795 to 1971. It even gave the street its name: Rue des Cordeliers became Rue de l'École-de-Médecine.
buildings.oldUse: Academy of Surgery / Faculty of Medicine
buildings.newUse: Head office of Paris Cité University

buildings.wiki: University of Paris Faculty of Law
buildings.name: Faculty of Law of Paris
buildings.description: Louis XV ordered a new home for the law faculty on the Place du Panthéon, and Jacques-Germain Soufflot, the Panthéon's own architect and a former law student here, designed it. It opened in 1774 and still serves law students today.
buildings.oldUse: Faculty of Law of the University of Paris

details.nickname: Home of the first permanent anatomical theatre
details.airportInfo: Venice Marco Polo is the nearest major airport. From there, buses and trains via Venice Mestre reach Padua.
details.funFact: The University of Padua has had its seat in the Palazzo del Bo since 1493, and inside it is the world's first permanent anatomical theatre, a model copied by universities across Europe.
details.languageInfo: Italian is the language of the city and of most teaching at the university.
details.transportationFact: The university's historic buildings are spread through Padua's old centre, so walking is the easiest way to see them. Trams and buses cover the longer hops.

buildings.name: Anatomical Theatre of Padua
buildings.description: Inaugurated in 1595 by Girolamo Fabrici of Acquapendente, this is the first permanent anatomical theatre in the world. It became the model for the anatomical theatres built at Europe's main universities in the 17th century.
buildings.newUse: Historic theatre in the Palazzo del Bo

buildings.name: Orto botanico di Padova
buildings.description: Founded in 1545, this is the world's oldest academic botanical garden still in its original place. Its plan is a perfect square inside an 84-metre circle, split into quarters by paths that point to the four compass directions. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

buildings.name: La Specola
buildings.description: A 14th-century castle tower that was turned into an astronomical observatory in 1767. Its lower observatory sits 16 metres up and its upper observatory 35 metres up, and the university used it until the 1930s.

buildings.name: Palazzo Maldura
buildings.description: This 16th-century palazzo was remodelled in 1769 by Giovan Battista Novello for the lawyer Andrea Maldura. Its rooms keep many frescoes, and today it houses the university's Department of Language Studies and Literature.

details.airportInfo: Brussels Airport is the closest major airport. Direct trains run from the airport station to Leuven.
details.funFact: KU Leuven bought the whole Great Beguinage in 1962 and spent 25 years restoring it, so a historic quarter of almost 100 houses is now university housing and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
details.languageInfo: Leuven is in Flanders, so Dutch is the local language, though many master's programmes are taught in English. The motto over the University Hall door is Latin: 'Wisdom has built herself a house'.
details.transportationFact: Leuven's centre is small and the university is everywhere in it, so walking or cycling is the norm.

buildings.name: University Hall, Leuven
buildings.description: Begun in 1317 as Leuven's cloth hall, it became the heart of the university, with an upper floor added in the 1680s for teaching and the library. Burned in the Sack of Leuven in 1914 and restored in the 1920s, it is now KU Leuven's main administrative building.

buildings.name: KU Leuven University Library
buildings.description: After the old library in University Hall burned in 1914, American architect Whitney Warren designed this new one on the Ladeuzeplein. Built between 1921 and 1928, it is a showpiece of neo-Flemish Renaissance style.

buildings.name: Great Beguinage, Leuven
buildings.description: A whole medieval quarter of brick houses, canals and bridges, once home to communities of beguines. The university bought it in 1962 and restored it street by street under Professor Raymond Lemaire, and its early Gothic church is the widest in town.

buildings.name: Arenberg Castle
buildings.description: This brick-and-sandstone château, finished in 1515, was home to the Arenberg family until the First World War. The university acquired it in 1921, and it is now the main building of the Faculty of Engineering, with architecture studios inside.

details.airportInfo: Helsinki Airport is Finland's main international airport. From central Helsinki, the metro runs west to Aalto University station in Otaniemi.
details.funFact: Alvar Aalto designed the key buildings of the Otaniemi campus, including the main building and the library, and the campus is listed as national cultural heritage of Finland.
details.languageInfo: Espoo is officially bilingual, so signs appear in Finnish and Swedish (Otaniemi is Otnäs in Swedish). Much of the university's teaching is in English.
details.transportationFact: Aalto University metro station sits right in the middle of campus, connected to the Väre building. Light rail line 15 also stops at the Korkeakouluaukio square.

buildings.name: Aalto University Undergraduate Center
buildings.description: Alvar Aalto designed this as the main building of the Helsinki University of Technology. The first part was completed in 1965 and the extension with the major auditoriums followed in 1975.
buildings.oldUse: Main building of Helsinki University of Technology

buildings.name: Dipoli
buildings.description: Reima and Raili Pietilä's Dipoli is a celebrated work of expressionist modernism, opened in 1966. Built for the Helsinki University of Technology's Student Union, it was sold to Aalto University in 2014.

buildings.name: Väre
buildings.description: Home of the School of Arts, Design and Architecture, Väre won its design contest in 2013 and opened in 2018 with a metro station beneath it. It was one of Finland's nominees for the EU Mies van der Rohe Award in 2019.
buildings.oldUse: School of Arts, Design and Architecture
buildings.newUse: School of Arts, Design and Architecture

buildings.name: Harald Herlin Learning Centre
buildings.description: The campus library is another Alvar Aalto design, a four-storey building completed in 1969. Renovated from 2015, it is now the Harald Herlin Learning Centre.

details.airportInfo: Arlanda, Stockholm's main airport, lies between Stockholm and Uppsala. Trains run from the airport north to Uppsala Central Station.
details.funFact: Carl Linnaeus owned the university's first botanical garden from 1741 and rearranged it to his own plan; it has been restored to look as it did in the 18th century.
details.languageInfo: Swedish is the local language, and many programmes are taught in English. Student life revolves around the 'nations', student societies named after regions of Sweden.
details.transportationFact: The historic university buildings cluster around the cathedral and University Park, all within a short walk of each other. Uppsala is also a famously bike-friendly city.

buildings.name: University Hall
buildings.description: Uppsala University's main building stands in University Park near the cathedral. Herman Teodor Holmgren designed it in an Italian Renaissance Beaux-Arts style, and it was completed in 1887.

buildings.name: Gustavianum
buildings.description: Built between 1622 and 1625, the Gustavianum is the oldest standing building of Uppsala University and was expanded by Olaus Rudbeck in 1662. It was the main university building from 1778 to 1887 and has been the university museum since 1997.
buildings.architect: Caspar van Panten; Olaus Rudbeck (1662 expansion)

buildings.name: Carolina Rediviva
buildings.description: Sweden's oldest and largest university library building was begun in 1820 and completed in 1841. It is where the Codex Argenteus, the 'Silver Bible', is kept.

buildings.name: Linnaean Garden
buildings.description: Olaus Rudbeck planted this garden in 1655, and Carl Linnaeus later owned it and rearranged it to his own design. Restored to his specifications, it is kept as an 18th-century botanical garden.
